title: Trump set to attend star-studded Irish Open at Doonbeg
description: BBC Sport looks ahead to the Irish Open with Rory McIlroy trying to defend the title and President Trump poised to attend.
fullText:
With the dust settling on Great Britain and Ireland's dramatic Walker Cup win at Lahinch, the action shifts 16 miles further down the west coast of Ireland as a quality field descends on Doonbeg for the 2026 Irish Open.

Twelve months ago, The K Club staged an Irish Open for the ages as home favourite Rory McIlroy captured his second title in dramatic fashion.

The six-time major winner again headlines a stellar field as Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in County Clare hosts the tournament for the first time.

The Irish Open precedes the tour's flagship event, the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth, which will be played next week.

With several star names in action and no shortage of storylines to follow throughout the week, here is everything you need to know about the Irish Open.

A lot. Five months after completing the career Grand Slam with a memorable win at the Masters, McIlroy sealed an emotional win in front of an ecstatic Irish crowd by beating Joakim Lagergren in a play-off.

Trailing Lagergren by two shots on the 72nd hole, McIlroy sunk a 25-foot eagle putt to take the Swede to a play-off and eventually prevailed on the third extra hole.

It was a gripping final round as McIlroy tussled for the trophy with Lagergren, overnight leader Adrien Saddier, Angel Hidalgo and Rafael Cabrera-Bello, who catapulted into contention with an ace at the third.

The win - which came nine years after his first Irish Open title - provided a well-timed boost for McIlroy just three weeks before he helped Europe retain the Ryder Cup with victory over the United States at Bethpage Black in New York.

While McIlroy will attract much of the attention in Doonbeg, he must fend off a high-quality field if he is to join European legends Seve Ballesteros, Nick Faldo, Bernhard Langer and Colin Montgomerie on three Irish Open wins.

As always, there is a strong Irish contingent. Shane Lowry, who memorably won his national title as an amateur in 2009, is chasing his first individual win in four years. The 2019 Open champion finished tied 15th last year.

Tom McKibbin arrives in decent form. The 23-year-old was in contention for last month's British Masters before a triple bogey early in the final round meant he had to settle for tied sixth.

Three-time major champion Padraig Harrington and two-time PGA Tour winner Seamus Power add further Irish interest.

Beyond the home hopes, there are a host of notable names. Two-time major winner Jon Rahm joins McIlroy in chasing a third Irish Open win after successes at Portstewart in 2017 and Lahinch two years later.

The Spaniard tees it up in Ireland amid ongoing uncertainty around LIV Golf's future. The breakaway tour, which launched in 2022, ended its season early following the withdrawal of the Public Investment Fund's financial backing.

McKibbin, England's Tyrrell Hatton and Chile's Joaquin Niemann are among the other LIV players in Ireland this week.

In addition, there is a strong European Ryder Cup flavour in the form of captain Luke Donald, Robert MacIntyre, Sepp Straka and twins Nicolai and Rasmus Hojgaard, who pipped McIlroy to the 2024 Irish Open at Royal County Down.

Five-time major winner Brooks Koepka also returns after missing the cut on his Irish Open debut last year.

US President Donald Trump - who owns the Doonbeg venue - is expected to attend the Irish Open.

Trump will be in Ireland this week as part of a two-day visit during which he will meet Irish President Catherine Connolly and hold a bilateral meeting with the Taoiseach [Irish prime minister] Micheal Martin.

He is expected to arrive in Ireland on Saturday and may present the Irish Open winner with the trophy on Sunday evening.

Donald Trump to meet Irish president on two day visit

The tee times will be released on Tuesday.

The Irish Open was first staged in 1927 and this week is the 71st edition of the event.

The tournament has been played at 21 courses across the island of Ireland, including renowned links venues Royal Portrush, Royal County Down and Portmarnock, which has hosted the tournament a record 19 times.

The cream of European talent competed during the 1980s and 1990s particularly.

Former winners include McIlroy, Rahm, Padraig Harrington, Sergio Garcia, Jose Maria Olazabal, Montgomerie, Faldo, Ian Woosnam, Ballesteros, Sam Torrance and Ben Crenshaw.

Formerly known simply as Doonbeg, the links course was designed by former world number one Greg Norman and opened in 2002.

It was redesigned by architect Martin Hawtree before the property was acquired by Trump in 2014 and renamed.

Unusually for a tour course, the layout boasts five par-fives and five par-threes. The signature hole is the par-three 14th, which can play as short as 111 yards.

title: Wigan captain Farrell to retire at end of season
description: Wigan Warriors captain Liam Farrell will retire at the end of the season after a 16-year career in which he has won 18 major honours.
fullText:
Wigan Warriors captain Liam Farrell, one of the game's most decorated players, will end his playing career after this season.

The second row forward has won six Super Leagues, five League Leaders' Shields, five Challenge Cups and the World Club Challenge on two occasions.

Farrell, 36, has scored 151 tries in 428 games for his hometown club since his debut in 2010.

He was made captain before the 2023 season and was the skipper when Wigan won an unprecedented quadruple in 2024.

Capped 12 times by England, Farrell was contracted until the end of next season but has not played since the end of June because of a shoulder injury.

"It's been a whirlwind of a career, more than I could ever have dreamed of doing," he told the club's website., external

"Although I'll be sad not to be playing any more, I'm also very grateful for the career I have had and I can now look forward to the next part of my life."

Wigan crush Leeds to move closer to winning shield

Farrell has a strong rugby league background, with his cousin being Wigan legend Andy, who is now head coach of Ireland's rugby union team.

Farrell came through the Warriors' academy system and made his debut as a teenager in April 2010.

Since then, the forward has only ever played for the Cherry and Whites - a pillar of consistency in the pack.

As well as the team honours, Farrell has been included in the Super League Dream Team on six occasions, while he was also the Harry Sunderland Trophy winner as player of the match in the 2016 Grand Final win over Warrington Wolves.

He was the natural replacement to succeed Thomas Leulaui as Wigan skipper and his quiet authority has been at the forefront of a new glorious era under head coach Matt Peet.

Farrell has won seven of the 11 trophies available to Wigan during his time as captain, the most recent being the Challenge Cup at Wembley in May.

He could add two more before he retires, as Wigan chase the League Leaders' Shield this week and the Grand Final next month.

"You have to make the right call at the right time, and I think I have done that," he said. "Speaking to people close to me, professionals and the advice I have been given, it's the right time.

"Playing one game for Wigan was always the goal for me. If I had have done that and never played again I'd have been immensely proud, my family would have been proud and we'd have gone back to being Wigan fans.

"So to have been able to play over 400 games in this jersey has been nothing short of incredible."

Wigan chief executive Kris Radlinski has confirmed Farrell will remain at the club in a strength and conditioning role once he stops playing, and he paid tribute to one of the Warriors' finest ever who will make the move from the pitch into the backroom team.

"Liam will go down as one of Wigan's greatest players," Radlinski said.

"Sustaining excellence for so many years requires extraordinary commitment, resilience and mental strength.

"He has always put the team first, carried himself with quiet humility, and earned the respect of everyone connected with the club. His legacy is secure and he deserves to be celebrated."

title: Smaller ball for women makes it 'harder to do my job'
description: A smaller ball is being trialled in women's international rugby union for September and October's WXV Global Series - and it is dividing opinion.
fullText:
England will play Australia, Canada and New Zealand in the next three weeks and, like all the world's top women's players, they have some new equipment: a smaller ball.

During September and October's WXV Global Series, World Rugby is trialling a size 4.5 ball - about 3% smaller than the size five used in the men's game, but the same weight.

Their introduction has not been without controversy and for England hooker May Campbell, responsible for throwing the ball in at the line-out, told BBC Sport it can go "a bit skew-whiff".

One of England's kickers, Helena Rowland, has found a much bigger margin for error with the smaller ball, saying: "If you get it slightly wrong, the difference is massive."

The fly-half says England players have noticed passes "dying", falling to the floor earlier than expected, "which they wouldn't have done previously".

Not all feedback has been negative. Wales wing Lisa Neumann is a fan, saying "it's changed the game" for her passing because of improved grip on the ball.

The thinking behind the trial is that the smaller ball will suit women's physiology and improve their skillset. In other sports, like basketball, women use a smaller ball, and in athletics sprint hurdles are lower for females.

But Rowland says she has never felt "hindered" by playing with the same size ball as in men's rugby.

Players with a specific skillset may find the change harder than others. Hookers must throw in at a line-out, scrum-halves are the most frequent passers and fly-halves the most regular kickers.

Rowland explained: "We've learned for however long how to kick with a size five.

"So I've had 13-odd years of doing that and training my routine and trying to nail that and get as much consistency as I can.

"So it's about, I suppose, trying to pack all those years of training and all those kicks into a four- or five-week block to get used to it, to then go out on to the world stage."

Rowland added that she has not "necessarily seen any positives", saying: "I know some of the girls have said that from an offload perspective, it's maybe made them more confident.

"But for me, it hasn't. I don't think there's enough of a change in the ball for me to be able to be running around with it in one hand and offloading left, right and centre.

"I haven't necessarily found any of the positive impacts. I've just found it a bit harder to do my job."

A World Rugby spokesperson said everyone involved in the WXV Global Series, including players, coaches and match officials, would have their views taken into account "with equal value" through surveys.

Smaller balls for women's rugby 'worst decision ever'

John Mitchell, England's head coach, has said "it's too early" to judge the impact of the smaller ball, and conclusions would have to be drawn after the world champions' opening three Tests in September.

Some England players were given a size 4.5 ball to practise with in the off-season and Campbell says "there's no point in complaining about it", given every side in the WXV Global Series will be in the same position.

But she adds: "I feel like a lot of us don't know how it's going to change the game, and kind of the reason behind it changing and the data behind it.

"It's just this decision has kind of just happened that we're now trialling it at the top level."

One area of concern for the England players is the ball changing shape.

Campbell says they "played around" with how much the ball was blown up, adding: "In previous weeks it was actually a bit fatter, and then this week it definitely feels smaller."

Rowland agrees, saying: "There needs to be a bit more done in terms of how the balls are made. We had some new balls today versus the ones we've had for the last three weeks [and the difference] is massive.

"If you've been training with an old ball that's fat to then go into a game and it's a completely different shape, actually that makes a massive difference as well, which I think is something that you don't necessarily find so much in the size five."

The ball has already been trialled in the Under-18s and Under-20s Women's Six Nations as well as the HSBC Sevens Series.

Rowland says she would "love to see the data on if it actually has made a difference".

It seems a fair request, and is one that BBC Sport put to World Rugby, but we did not receive any data.

A spokesperson said: "The balls haven't been used in the international XVs environment yet so there isn't directly comparable data to share with players either directly or via their unions.

"Once we've built up a large enough data set of player responses, match official responses and game data, we'll publish the results, so it'll be available to players, unions, the International Rugby Players Association, coaches, match officials, the media and everyone else."

Some players are frustrated as they feel they have become guinea pigs on the global stage. To compound that frustration, they will then return to their clubs where the league season will be played with a size five ball once again.

BBC Sport asked World Rugby when the trial period is likely to conclude, and were told: "We'll be able to assess our position on women's 15s once the international window has started.

"This will allow for completion of the WXV tournaments and full analysis in early 2027. The evidence to date suggests that further exposure produces greater results."

While it looks like players and coaches will get to see the data in early 2027, any wider outcomes or decisions might take longer.

title: How £725 game-show winnings kick-started Champions League coach's career
description: Lithuanian coach Valdas Dambrauskas cut his teeth in English football, and now returns in the Champions League with Sabah.
fullText:
On Thursday, Valdas Dambrauskas will walk out at Old Trafford as manager of Sabah in the Champions League.

The Lithuanian's career will come full circle, some 20 years since he made his first steps into coaching with Manchester United Soccer Schools.

"This is beyond my imagination," Dambrauskas told BBC Sport. "To go through that tunnel on to that pitch.

"I've been many times to Old Trafford with the kids, and now I'm going to come as a coach."

This only scratches the surface of Dambrauskas' remarkable story.

It begins with an appearance on the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, Dambrauskas using his modest winnings to move to London and forge a career in football.

It is a tale of casual jobs, a determination to succeed and a nomadic coaching career across Europe - which now brings the 49-year-old back to England in the Champions League with the Azerbaijani club.

As Sabah's players and staff celebrated reaching the Champions League two weeks ago, unbeknownst to Dambrauskas he was becoming a social media star.

It all related to that appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? in 2002.

Not because he was on the show, but how he spent the money he won.

"This is so long ago," said Dambrauskas with a wry smile. "A back-in-the-year story that really was forgotten.

"And now suddenly everybody is speaking about this."

Dambrauskas walked away with 4,000 litas (about £725). That might not sound like much, but it was six months' wages to the average Lithuanian.

For Dambrauskas, the real story should be his career and not a game show.

"Everybody now takes only this part, you know, about the money," Dambrauskas said. "But yes, it is a true story.

"My idea was somehow I will try to go on these [coaching] courses to gain the coaching badge, maybe go back one day to Lithuania and start to work as a football coach."

What began with Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? would map out his whole career.

Dambrauskas says he had known since the age of 12 he would not make it as a player, but coaching would keep him close to football.

He arrived in London in August 2002 aged 25 on a student visa with limited English.

What followed would be eight years of hard work where he would coach for community projects, at a semi-professional club, within professional youth programmes - and hold down multiple jobs while raising two children.

In 2004 he enrolled on a course in sports science and coaching at London Metropolitan University, the first real step in his career.

Then he started out coaching by volunteering with the Access to Sports Project for deprived children in Finsbury Park.

He went on to work with London Tigers, a charitable community organisation which runs teams from junior level right through to semi-professional.

Starting out as a volunteer, across five years he progressed to manage the first team in non-league football in the Spartan South Midlands League, FA Cup and FA Vase.

Dambrauskas became the first Lithuanian to achieve a Uefa coaching licence through the London Football Association.

"I went on every possible course, every possible conference, London Football Coaches Association meetings," Dambrauskas said.

"Everywhere I could go just to gain some information, some knowledge, some extra diploma, extra course.

"That was very important for me and I took my chances."

He got his first break at a professional club when Manchester United Soccer Schools took a chance on him in 2004.

Dambrauskas spent five years coaching on residential courses in the UK and in Europe.

"That was the best thing that could happen in my life," Dambrauskas said.

"I went through three or four interviews. I will be forever grateful to [Foundation chief executive] John Shiels, the way he gave me this chance, because I didn't have experience.

"I'd never been in a place with so many great personalities as I got in the Manchester United Soccer Schools."

After a short spell with Fulham, Dambrauskas moved to Brentford. He credits academy director Ose Aibangee as one of the biggest influences on his career, pushing his limits.

All the while he was juggling home life and working multiple jobs to make ends meet.

"I was a gardener, a handyman, doing newspaper rounds at the beginning, also polishing floors in a pub," Dambrauskas said.

"So many jobs. Working in retail, and then as a sports development officer, then a sports development manager, and the central YMCA.

"I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs."

As well as the trip to Manchester United this week, Sabah will complete their Champions League group games at Arsenal in January.

This also feels like fate for Dambrauskas - one of the buildings at London Metropolitan University on Holloway Road overlooked Emirates Stadium.

When asked about his time in England, Dambrauskas' face lights up.

"When I hear this word 'England', it for me sounds like opportunities," Dambrauskas said.

"It was really amazing. England gave me all this and I'll forever be grateful."

Dambrauskas was working three jobs - at Brentford, London Tigers and as a sports development manager - when the opportunity arose to coach full-time.

It meant leaving England to return to Lithuania, champions Ekranas appointing him assistant first-team and reserve-team coach at the end of 2010.

After four years at Ekranas he was named manager of Zalgiris Vilnius, Lithuania's biggest club, where his career really took off.

Dambrauskas won two league titles, three Lithuanian Cups and two Lithuanian Super Cups across three seasons - including a treble in 2016.

Then came a series of moves in which Dambrauskas took charge of eight teams over nine years in seven countries.

First RFS, with whom he won the Latvian Cup, and then Gorica in Croatia.

A third league title came with Bulgarian side Ludogorets Razgrad, along with another Super Cup and Europa League qualification.

Dambrauskas then returned to Croatia with Hajduk Split, a time which he described as "absolutely amazing" as the club won the Croatian Cup - their first trophy for 10 years.

Next up was a spell in Greece with OFI Crete, then Omonia in Cyprus - who qualified for the Conference League - and Diosgyori in Hungary.

Finally, in the summer of 2025, he arrived at Sabah, the 10th club of his career.

Dambrauskas completed the league and cup double in his first season, as the club won the title for the first time.

It took his trophy tally to 13 across five countries.

Next stop, the Champions League.

Dambrauskas had to navigate four knockout ties to get Sabah to the Champions League, and they are the only club to make it all the way through from the first qualifying round.

Welsh club TNS, Finland's KuPS, Danish side Aarhus and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were all knocked out.

The final qualifying game was as dramatic as Dambrauskas' own story.

Sabah were going out, then a goal by Tellur Mutallimov in the fourth minute of stoppage time sent the tie into extra time. They went on to win 5-2 on the night and 6-4 on aggregate.

"To go to the Champions League is something beyond imagination," Dambrauskas said.

"We have never qualified for the Conference League, we have never qualified for the Europa League. We have never passed more than two rounds in a row in one competition, and now suddenly we are here."

Sabah are based in the town of Masazir - 30 miles north of the Azerbaijan capital Baku - with a population of just 19,000.

Known as the Owls, Sabah were only formed in 2017 and on Tuesday will celebrate their ninth birthday.

Like many small clubs, their Bank Respublika Arena home, with a capacity of less than 9,000, does not meet Uefa regulations. Instead, the club are expected to play their matches at the Olympic Stadium in Baku.

Sabah will host Borussia Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli, and face a trip to Villarreal - as well as the visits to England.

"It can be a very hard draw, and it can be a Sabah draw," said Dambrauskas, clearly excited by the prospect.

"You dream for this, to play in this competition, to play against those teams.

"So now is the time to show that you can handle it, to find a way to compete and we will try to do this.

"We have a good team, we have an ambitious team, we have hungry players who are really keen to show themselves."

Sabah president Magsud Adigozalov last week was full of praise for Dambrauskas' impact.

"His influence goes beyond tactics," Adigozalov told Report. "He has instilled a mindset and winning mentality in the team.

"Even in the most difficult moments, the team never abandons its game or fighting spirit, which is the result of the coach's work."

Twenty years ago, Dambrauskas looked out over the pitch at Old Trafford during one of his job interviews, dreaming that one day he would stand in one of the dugouts.

Now his coaching career will return to where it started.

"I lived in England when the battle between Manchester United and Arsenal was the biggest rivalry. Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger," Dambrauskas said.

"Now I'm going to come back as a coach in the Champions League and hear that anthem. It's really amazing."

title: Fury says he is looking for new opponent, calls out Usyk
description: Tyson Fury has sparked more speculation his all-British heavyweight fight with Anthony Joshua is on the verge of collapse by suggesting he needs a new opponent for November.
fullText:
Tyson Fury claims he is looking for a new opponent for November and has called out Oleksandr Usyk despite being contracted to fight Anthony Joshua next.

The all-British heavyweight showdown is being targeted for November, with both Joshua and Fury signing individual contracts for the contest.

But the issue of where the fight takes place has caused a delay in an official announcement with organisers pushing to stage it in the US rather than Joshua's preferred location of Wembley Stadium.

In an expletive-laden video posted on Instagram, Fury claimed Joshua was backing out of the fight.

"This will only lead me to a fight with Oleksandr Usyk," he said.

"Oleksandr you're his [Joshua's] trainer and his sensei and you know he is weak minded... and that he would never fight the Gypsy King which you have had the guts to do twice.

"You got the decisions last time, fair play to you.

"Good luck to you, let's do it again. Let's run it back in November. The ball is now in your court... do you want to fight me this year, 2026, or are you calling it quits?

"Let me know because I am now looking for a new opponent."

Fury has twice lost to Usyk, with the two-time undisputed heavyweight champion now working with Joshua as part of his training and coaching team.

Sela, Queensberry and Matchroom declined to comment on whether talks had broken down when contacted by BBC Sport.

We want Fury v Joshua at Wembley - London mayor

Taylor's 'dream ending to a dream career'

Saudi Arabian promoter Sela is fronting the bill for the prospective Joshua-Fury fight, with both men signing separate contracts with the company.

Joshua's contract stipulates it must take place in the UK, leading to his promoter Eddie Hearn renegotiating details in that deal.

But after London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan made a public plea for the fight to happen at Wembley, Hearn said talks about staging it in the UK had "re-opened".

Sela and broadcaster Netflix are understood to favour New York's Madison Square Garden.

BBC Sport understands Sela has contacted the London mayor's office in recent weeks about bringing the long-awaited contest to the national stadium, but have not progressed talks further since last week.

Hearn had said he hoped an announcement could happen in the coming week, but that now seems unlikely given the latest developments.

A bout at Wembley may need to happen in the early hours - which would draw in a larger television audience in the US.

Khan says his team would back such a proposal.

"A message to the promoters - we want to host it in London. Talk to us, we're really keen to have it," Khan told BBC Sport on Thursday.

"I'm hoping the promoters understand that not only will you get 100,000 people watching this bout live, you'll get millions watching it across the globe, where both boxers are cheered on by their loyal fans."

title: Pietersen joins England's white-ball coaching team
description: England appoint former Ashes-winning batter Kevin Pietersen to their white-ball coaching team in the build-up to the 2027 ICC Cricket World Cup.
fullText:
England have appointed former Ashes-winning batter Kevin Pietersen to their white-ball coaching team in the build-up to the 2027 ICC Cricket World Cup.

Pietersen, 46, joins as a specialist mentor and will start in the role for the upcoming T20 and one-day matches against Sri Lanka.

He will also be involved in this winter's tours to Australia and South Africa, before joining up with the teams again for the home series against Pakistan and New Zealand next summer, as well as the 50-over World Cup, which is being held in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia in the autumn.

"I've got immense respect for KP and what he's achieved in the game," said England's white-ball head coach Brendon McCullum.

"He's had an amazing impact on English cricket, so for someone with his experience, knowledge and stature to want to play a role with this team is a fantastic result."

Pietersen is one of England's most successful white-ball batters, being named player of the tournament when they won the T20 World Cup for the first time in 2010.

The right-hander scored almost 4,500 ODI runs at an average of 41.32 - bettered only by Joe Root - while in T20 cricket he has the highest average of all batters to hit more than 1,000 runs for England.

He did, however, fall out with a number of former England players and coaches during his career.

He was accused of being "divisive" in the dressing room and was dropped during a Test series against South Africa in 2012 for sending "provocative" text messages to opposing players, for which he apologised to then captain Andrew Strauss.

He was only allowed to return to the team after a successful 'reintegration' period.

Pietersen was also one of the first to advocate for England players being allowed to play in the Indian Premier League and other white-ball franchise leagues around the world - a stance which often put him at odds with his employers.

Since retiring, Pietersen has enjoyed a successful career as a commentator and content creator while he has mentored in the Indian Premier League for Delhi Capitals.

"I am immensely proud to have been asked to help this team on their journey to win a World Cup in South Africa," said Pietersen.

"Putting on the England uniform again for the first time since 2014 is a profound honour and a deeply special moment.

"We have an incredibly talented white-ball squad, and I am excited to get in the trenches and work relentlessly hard with these players to maximise their potential."

Pietersen spoke about his coaching ambitions earlier in 2026,, external after England's 4-1 Ashes hammering in Australia.

Though this role is with the white-ball teams, he said he would "love" to help coach the Test side, telling the Guardian he has "got all the credentials" and has "worn every ​single T-shirt".

Hinting at his approach, he added: "In the shortest ‌form ⁠of the game, sure, play without fear, go out there, be brave, be reckless, be careless, be whatever you want. In Test match cricket, you cannot do that."

He also criticised England's coaching set-up, led by McCullum, during a white-ball tour to India in 2025.

"I'm sorry, but I am absolutely gobsmacked that England did not have one team practice session since losing the first ODI and losing the T20 series," said Pietersen, who was working as a commentator for the host broadcaster.

Pietersen's first assignment will be a three-match T20 series against Sri Lanka, which begins on 15 September in Southampton.

This is quite a return to international cricket for a man who was effectively fired by England 12 years ago.

After all the animosity and acrimony that followed the end of Kevin Pietersen's playing career at the very highest level, he is back with the Three Lions on his chest.

For England, this is the first step in reshaping the backroom teams in the new era of split coaches. It is also not the first time they have hired a big name to act as a consultant to the white-ball side, following Andrew Flintoff and Kieron Pollard.

In terms of intrigue, the appointment of Pietersen outstrips anything that has come before.

Perhaps the greatest white-ball batter to play for England, his knowledge and experience will bring an X-factor to the coaching staff.

It's also a smart move given his expertise of playing in South Africa, the venue of the next 50-over World Cup. Who could forget Pietersen announcing himself as an international cricketer in the country of his birth in 2005, smashing runs against the Proteas in a one-day series?

What could Pietersen bring to the game of Harry Brook, for example? Brook is the closest England have produced to another Pietersen, yet has admitted he still needs to make better decisions in the middle. It was a criticism Pietersen often faced during his career.

Along with Brook, the England dressing room is filled with players who grew up watching and idolising Pietersen. There should be a queue of batters wanting to work with him.

But there will also be a nagging doubt over whether this could go wrong at any moment. Pietersen is not shy of speaking his mind, or clashing with authority. He joins a dressing room run by Brendon McCullum, another big personality.

Either way, it promises to be box-office stuff.

An unforgettable, unreliable, idiosyncratic genius - England should be grateful for Pietersen

Pietersen - the unanswered questions

title: K2 Horizon
description: Every model is released fully open, with weights, code, training data, and methodology, allowing researchers, developers, and institutions worldwide to inspect, reproduce, and adapt them.
fullText:
The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI) today launched K2 Horizon, a fleet of six AI foundation models ranging from 0.9 billion to 375 billion parameters. Every model is released fully open, with weights, code, training data, and methodology, allowing researchers, developers, and institutions worldwide to inspect, reproduce, and adapt them.

Across reasoning, mathematics, coding and agentic tasks, K2 Horizon delivers top-tier performance in every size class, with the 0.9B, 3.7B and 7B models setting new state of the art at their respective scales. The 0.9B model is designed for highly constrained environments such as watches and glasses, while the 3.7B and 7B models bring advanced capabilities to phones and other on-device applications. The dense 32B model and sparse 36B-A4B model provide powerful options for local hosting and on-premise servers, and the 375B-A23B model brings the fleet’s strongest capabilities to demanding enterprise deployments.

K2 Horizon is the largest fully open model release in AI history, and it cements the UAE’s leadership in building frontier-grade AI systems that are developed by national institutions and shared openly with the world. The launch gives developers and researchers greater choice in capabilities, scale and deployment options. While most releases described as “open” stop at publishing weights, the K2 family has moved progressively toward end-to-end transparency, a trajectory that began with K2, continued through K2-Think and K2 Think V2, and reaches its widest expression with K2 Horizon.

The six models share a core architecture, vocabulary, training methodology, interfaces and deployment tooling, with a smaller vocabulary for the 0.9B model. IFM’s dynamic model routing technique directs tasks to the most cost-effective model and provides developers with a practical path from prototype to production. The fully open code, training data and recipes are a significant step forward in transparency, well beyond the “open weights” dialogue that has dominated AI industry headlines over recent weeks.

Professor Eric Xing, Founder of IFM, and President and University Professor of MBZUAI, said: “We believe meaningful AI progress depends on the ability to examine, build upon, and improve the technology, not simply access it through an API. The most important technology of our time should be built with the world, not kept from it. K2 Horizon is what that conviction looks like when an institution commits to it completely, and it reflects the environment we work in here in the UAE: a country that decided to build AI rather than wait for it.”

K2 Horizon includes key technology innovations: 1) A unique “diffusion distillation” technique that generates blocks of tokens in parallel, which speeds model performance by roughly 3X without degrading response quality and 2) A “mixture of value attention” architecture that improves reasoning without adding more computation; and 3) Dynamic model routing, which directs tasks to the most cost-effective model and provides developers with a practical path from prototype to production.

K2 Horizon’s three smallest models achieve state-of-the-art results in their respective classes across mathematics, reasoning, software-engineering and agentic capabilities.

Each K2 Horizon model is engineered to compete with the best open models of its size on reasoning, tool use, and agentic tasks. The smallest is built for devices where memory, power consumption and local processing matter; the largest for demanding reasoning and enterprise workloads. Developers can prototype on one and scale to another without changing model architecture or workflows.

Hector Liu, Director of IFM’s Silicon Valley Research Lab, said: “Rather than release a single model, we’re releasing an entire fleet at once, six models, from one small enough to run on a watch to a flagship built for enterprise reasoning. Every model is built to compete with the best open models at its size, and everyone ships with the weights, code, training data, and methodology behind it. Developers can prototype on the smallest model, scale to the flagship, and verify every claim we make along the way.”

The launch of K2 Horizon also marks IFM’s continued growth as a global AI research lab operating from Abu Dhabi. Established in May 2025, IFM now employs AI researchers, scientists and developers across three offices in Abu Dhabi, Silicon Valley and Paris, a distribution that places frontier model development in the UAE while drawing talent from the world’s leading AI centers.

Today, MBZUAI is an integral part of the UAE’s AI transformation, training 80,000 federal employees as agentic AI experts under a strategic knowledge partnership with the Federal Authority for Government Human Resources. K2 Horizon extends that role into research: models built for reasoning, tool use, and agentic tasks.

K2 Horizon models are available immediately through Hugging Face, as well as vLLM and SGLang. The API of K2 Horizon is available today through IFM’s global ecosystem of inference partners, including Compass, Cerebras, AWS and Nebius. K2 Horizon models and code are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

title: 10-task GLM 5.3 harness bench: Claude, OpenCode, pi, zcode, Hermes and 3code
description: Sharing technical knowledge from doing grunt programming work wh
fullText:
I'm performing a series of harness benchmarks on the same 10 SWE-bench verified tasks representatively chosen for difficulty. This is far from a perfect measure and unpublished model improvements mean that results are far from deterministic, but it does allow for a rough evaluation without breaking the bank. As with all benchmarks- use your own heuristics to confirm! Use the harness and check your feel- do you get a sense you getting more mileage? That's what counts because it's what you can actually measure.

Having said that, this sort of benchmarks have been positively great for spotting harness blunders.

Note that none of these results, even when taken with a grain of salt, mean you should necessarily choose one harness over another. If you have an unlimited budget and just like Claude Code, by all means go for it. But if you want absolute maximum savings and you like very terse command line agents- give 3code a try!

In the graphic there are 5 columns- harness name (the latest at time of writing was chosen), amount of solved tasks of the 10, an indication of used tokens as well as total tokens, cache rate, and percentage of tokens used relative to the winner.

The picture is pretty drastic- 3code used 5 million tokens and solved 9 of the 10 tasks. The runner up in token usage is pi, which only solved 6 of the 10 tasks in the allotted time- the runner up in completed tasks is opencode, the only other harness to solve 9 of 10 tasks ('astropi' is the hard one that can be flipped).

zcode was hyper efficient on the tasks it was successful at, but dug its heels in on the tasks it was unsuccessful at and used a lot of tokens before timing out. Hermes was expensive and did okay- I suppose that's a pretty good result since it is not strictly a coding model and more of an agentic model where cheaper models to moderate difficulty coding to expand capabilities.

As expected, Claude Code positively splurges tokens, consistent with Anthropic's hyper maximalist approach to all aspects of performance. That it didn't get astropi might have been bad luck.

opencode's excellent cache rate is notable- however, given it uses twice the tokens, it's still the more expensive choice. Personally, in most of my projects, cached tokens are the largest expense so I believe in reducing overall token usage more than in increasing cache rate. After all, if you have more tokens used again and again, there is a greater opportunity to cache but then it still costs. Having said that- this test certainly informs 3code development towards finding unnecessarily uncached tokens and 99.2% on an independent benchmark is very impressive. Our lowly 95% numbers might still be good enough though!

pi continues to impress how far it can go without having model specific tuning, but I do feel that the 3code approach of having a model family specific system prompt and also finetuning was shown to be paying off. I think what's happening is that this run's 3code version benefitted from stealing all the zcode GLM 5.3 specific finetuning, but then not having the overly aggressive task completion policy.

I intend to continue to create harness benchmarks and am working on funding more extensive tests, and also different kinds of tests- cost is the limiting factor right now since I'm independent and not associated with any provider.

The tokens for this test were provided by Zhipu's startup program, but they didn't influence the results in any way- they gave me the tokens and cut me loose. I also converged on GLM as the main 3code dev tool first, and asked them to give me tokens second. But I'm still interested in doing tests with other companies as well, Zhipu was just the first to give a positive response to my requests. Thank you!
